title: A trajectory with velocity arrows: where does it go and how fast?
summary: The path of a body in the plane, with arrows showing its velocity at equal time steps. With and without air drag on one plot, the arrows show how drag shortens the range and steepens the descent.

media.alt: Two arched trajectories in a wide equal-scale plot: a taller dashed blue arch reaching 40 metres, and a shorter solid teal arch with drag landing at 25 metres, each with markers and small arrows along the path.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where does it go and how fast?
read_the_figure.axes: x: horizontal distance in metres, 0 to 42. y: height in metres, -1 to 21. Equal scale, so angles are true. Arrows: velocity at equal time steps, drawn at 1 m/s = 1/6 m. Dashed blue: no drag. Solid teal: quadratic drag with coefficient 0.02 per metre.
look_at: Compare the two ranges and the two maximum heights.
Is the drag path symmetric about its highest point? Compare ascent with descent.
How do the arrows change along each path: length (speed) and direction?
What is the horizontal part of the velocity at the top of the no-drag path?
as_drawn: Launch speed 20 m/s at 50 degrees. Without drag: range 40.2 m, peak 11.96 m, flight 3.12 s. With drag (numerical, step 0.002 s): range 25.0 m, peak 9.0 m, flight 2.7 s.
Markers are at equal time steps, so their spacing shows speed; the arrows show velocity at those markers at a scale of 1/6 m per m/s.
A note in the corner gives the arrow scale. The two paths start together and separate as drag acts; the drag path descends more steeply than it climbs.
read_the_figure.proves: The shapes and size of the two paths for these parameters. It does not show how the drag coefficient was chosen or how sensitive the range is to it.
if_wrong: Unequal axis scales: launch and landing angles look wrong.
Arrows with no stated scale: speeds cannot be read.
Markers at equal distance rather than equal time: the spacing says nothing about speed.

terms.meaning: The path of a body through space.
The rate of change of position; tangent to the path, with length equal to speed.
Horizontal distance at landing, maximum height, and total time in the air.
A resistive force proportional to the square of the speed and opposite to the velocity.
The steady speed at which drag balances weight in vertical fall.
Dots at fixed time steps, so spacing along the path gives speed.

remember: Vacuum: R = v0^2 sin 2 theta / g, H = v0^2 sin^2 theta / 2g, T = 2 v0 sin theta / g.
Velocity is tangent to the path; its length is the speed.
Equal axes, arrow scale stated, markers at equal time steps.
Drag makes the path asymmetric: steeper on the way down.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The line is the path, so position carries the trajectory itself. Dots show where the body is at equal times. Arrows at the dots show the velocity: direction and size on a stated scale. Dash style and colour separate the two cases.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: The question has two parts: where (the path) and how fast (the velocity). The path alone has no speed in it; putting arrows at equal-time dots adds it. Overlaying the no-drag path as a reference shows what drag does by difference: a shorter, lower, asymmetric arch. Equal axes keep the launch angle and the descent angle true.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Unequal axes turn the angles into lies. Arrows that mix units (m/s drawn as metres) are hard to compare with the path's scale. Markers at unequal time steps give the wrong impression of speed. The two cases end at different times, so they have different numbers of arrows. And the numerical drag path depends on the integrator and its step.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: Equal axes give honest angles. The drag-versus-no-drag overlay shows the effect and its size at once. Together with the arrow scale they let the reader quote ranges, heights and speeds without further data.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For a time view plot x(t), y(t) (F4.4). For speed plot |v| against t. For energy see F4.5. For the whole family of launch angles plot range against angle. For the speed-direction relation plot the hodograph, v_y against v_x.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a third path for 0.05 per metre drag, mark the moments of peak height with a dot on each path, and draw the arrow at landing so that the landing angle can be read.

steps.title: Vacuum formulas
steps.note: For v0 = 20 m/s, theta = 50 degrees, g = 9.81: R = 40.16 m, H = 11.96 m, T = 3.12 s. The render's dashed path ends at about 40 m and peaks at 12 m.

steps.title: Adding quadratic drag
steps.note: No closed form for the plane path; integrated numerically it gives R = 25.0 m, H = 9.02 m, T = 2.71 s. The launch speed 20 m/s is close to the terminal speed 22.1 m/s, so drag is strong.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) by how much does drag shorten the range? (2) What is the speed at the top of the no-drag path? (3) Is the drag path symmetric?

solution.text: From about 40 m to about 25 m: 38 percent shorter.
At the top the vertical velocity is zero, so only the horizontal part remains: 20 cos 50 degrees = 12.9 m/s, an arrow of length 12.9 / 6 = 2.1 m in the picture.
No: the descent is steeper than the ascent, because drag has removed horizontal speed.

worked.answer: Range reduced by about 38 percent; 12.9 m/s horizontal at the top (no drag); the drag path is asymmetric.

analyze.q: The drag trajectory is steeper on the way down. Explain with the horizontal and vertical velocity components.
analyze.hint: Drag acts on both components, but gravity keeps accelerating the vertical one.

analyze.q: Why are equal-time markers needed for speed?
analyze.hint: Equal arc length markers would hide it.

analyze.q: What would the arrows look like at the landing point for the drag case compared with the no-drag case?

evaluate.q: Sports coaches quote a '45 degree optimal angle'. What does this plot say about that rule when air drag is present?
evaluate.hint: Optimal angle with drag is below 45 degrees; try several angles.

create: Plot range against launch angle for k = 0 and k = 0.02 on one axis.
Add the hodograph (v_y against v_x) of each path as a second panel.

checks.q: Why does a drag-free path form a symmetric arch?
checks.answer: Only gravity acts, which gives a parabola symmetric about the peak; with drag horizontal speed decays so the descent is steeper.

checks.q: v0 = 20 m/s at 50 degrees in vacuum: range?
Two trajectories differ only in drag but end at different times. Why must the markers be at equal time steps?
checks.answer: At equal time steps the spacing between markers is proportional to speed; at equal distance steps the markers would say nothing about speed.
